analogy.p: Think of a road between two towns that goes over a hill. Driving from town A (high up) down to town B (lower) releases energy, because you roll downhill and the car gets warm brakes (exothermic). Driving back from B to A means climbing the same hill and using fuel, taking in exactly the same amount of energy (endothermic). The traffic can go both ways on the same road, and the number of cars in each direction depends on the conditions, such as a road toll or a traffic jam (temperature or concentration). The analogy breaks down because real chemical reactions involve particles rearranging bonds, not vehicles on a fixed road.
analogy.t: A two-way street with a hill

bullets: In a reversible reaction the **products can react to form the original reactants**.
The two directions are called the **forward reaction** and the **reverse reaction**.
A reversible reaction is shown with the symbol **⇌** (two half-arrows pointing in opposite directions), not with a single arrow →.
General form: **A + B ⇌ C + D**: A and B react to form C and D, and C and D can react to re-form A and B.
Whether the forward or the reverse reaction is favoured depends on the **conditions**, such as temperature, pressure and concentrations.
Most reactions you meet at GCSE (such as combustion, rusting or neutralisation) are treated as going **one way only**, so only specific examples are shown with ⇌.
Be ready to give at least two examples: **hydrated copper(II) sulfate** and the **Haber process** (and ammonium chloride heating).
core.p: In many chemical reactions the products cannot easily turn back into the reactants, so the reaction is described as going one way only. In a **reversible reaction**, however, the **products can react to produce the original reactants**. This means the same reaction can run in two directions: the **forward reaction** turns reactants into products and the **reverse reaction** turns products back into reactants. Reversible reactions matter because they explain why some industrial processes, such as the Haber process, never convert all the reactants into product, and they lead into the idea of dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle.

bullets: Use **⇌** between the two sides; never use = or a single → for a reversible reaction in an exam answer.
Example: **N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)** (the Haber process).
Example: **hydrated copper(II) sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water**: CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l or g).
Example: **NH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + HCl(g)**.
The equation must be **balanced** in the same way as any other equation: the same number of each type of atom on both sides.
Writing ⇌ does not mean the two reactions are happening at equal speeds; it only shows reversibility (equal rates happen at **equilibrium**, covered in the next topic).
If a question asks you to complete or balance a reversible equation, balance first, then draw the ⇌ symbol.
core.h: Writing reversible reactions: the equilibrium arrow
core.p: A reversible reaction is shown in an equation using the symbol **⇌**. Everything to the left of the symbol is the reactants of the forward reaction and everything on the right is the products of the forward reaction, but because the reaction can go both ways, either side can act as the reactants. The equation must still be **balanced**, and **state symbols** are included when you are told them (for example N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)). The symbol does not say how far the reaction goes in either direction, only that both directions can occur.

bullets: **Heating** favours the **endothermic** direction because it supplies the energy that direction needs.
**Cooling** (or removing heat) favours the **exothermic** direction.
**Adding a reactant or removing a product** can drive the reaction in one direction (for example removing steam from a test tube).
In a **closed system** nothing can enter or leave, so both directions can occur and the reaction can reach equilibrium.
In an **open system** the products can escape, so the reverse reaction may not happen (for example the gases escape from an open test tube).
The same chemicals can be turned into each other repeatedly: this is the key feature that distinguishes a reversible reaction from a normal one-way reaction.
Higher tier link: Le Chatelier's principle predicts how changing conditions shifts the position of equilibrium.
core.h: Changing the direction by changing conditions
core.p: One of the most important ideas in this topic is that the **direction of a reversible reaction can be changed by changing the conditions**. For example, heating hydrated copper sulfate drives the forward reaction (water is lost), while adding water to anhydrous copper sulfate drives the reverse reaction. Similarly, heating ammonium chloride causes it to break down into ammonia and hydrogen chloride, while cooling the gases lets them react together again to form ammonium chloride. The conditions decide which direction is favoured, and in practice both reactions may occur at the same time.

bullets: If the forward reaction is **exothermic** (ΔH negative), the reverse reaction is **endothermic** (ΔH positive).
If the forward reaction is **endothermic**, the reverse reaction is **exothermic**.
The **size** of the energy change is the **same** in both directions; only the sign (direction of energy transfer) changes.
Example: Haber process forward reaction ΔH = −92 kJ/mol (exothermic), so the reverse (ammonia breaking down) is **+92 kJ/mol** (endothermic) for the equation as written.
**Exothermic** = energy **released** to the surroundings; the thermometer reading **goes up**.
**Endothermic** = energy **absorbed** from the surroundings; the thermometer reading **goes down**.
This is a **conservation of energy** idea: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.
core.p: AQA states that **if a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction, and the same amount of energy is transferred in each case**. An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings (the temperature of the surroundings rises), whereas an endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings (the temperature falls). This follows from the conservation of energy: going from reactants to products releases a certain amount of energy, so getting back from products to reactants needs exactly the same amount to be put in.

bullets: Forward exothermic: **products lower** than reactants; ΔH is **negative**.
Reverse endothermic: **products (original reactants) higher**; ΔH is **positive** and equal in size.
Both reactions share the **same peak** (the same transition state energy).
Activation energy of reverse = activation energy of forward + size of ΔH (for an exothermic forward reaction).
A **catalyst lowers the peak** and so lowers the activation energy for **both** directions equally.
Label axes: **Energy** (vertical) and **Progress of reaction** (horizontal).
Check: forward Ea = 60 kJ/mol and ΔH = −40 kJ/mol gives reverse Ea = 60 + 40 = **100 kJ/mol**.
core.h: Reaction profiles for the forward and reverse reactions
core.p: A reaction profile for the forward reaction of an exothermic reversible reaction shows reactants at a higher energy than products. If you read the same diagram from right to left, you are looking at the reverse reaction, which starts at the low energy of the products, climbs the same hill and finishes at the higher energy of the reactants, so it is endothermic. For a Higher-tier style question you should note that the **activation energy of the reverse reaction is larger** than that of the forward reaction for an exothermic forward reaction, because the reverse reaction starts lower down and has to climb further to the same peak.

bullets: Equation: **CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O**.
Blue (hydrated) → white (anhydrous) on **heating**: **endothermic**; steam is seen escaping or condensing on the cooler glass.
White (anhydrous) → blue on **adding water**: **exothermic**; the mixture gets warm.
This colour change is used as a **chemical test for water**: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue if water is present.
It is a test for the **presence** of water but not for pure water, because other solutions containing water also turn it blue.
**Hydrated** means containing water of crystallisation; **anhydrous** means containing no water.
Water of crystallisation is water that is part of the crystal structure, in a fixed ratio (here five molecules of water per formula unit of CuSO₄).
core.p: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is a **blue crystalline solid** whose crystals contain water of crystallisation. When it is heated the water is driven off as steam and the solid changes to a **white powder**, **anhydrous copper(II) sulfate**. This forward reaction is **endothermic** because heat is needed to drive the water out. If water is added to the white powder, it turns **blue again** and heat is released, so the reverse reaction is **exothermic** (the test tube gets noticeably warm). The same amount of energy is transferred in each direction, and the reaction can be repeated many times.

bullets: Equation: **NH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + HCl(g)**.
**Heating** the solid causes the **forward** reaction (decomposition), which is **endothermic**.
**Cooling** the gases causes the **reverse** reaction (recombination), which is **exothermic**.
The reaction is done in a test tube that is open at the top, so some gas escapes: it is not a closed system.
Observation: **white solid** at the bottom disappears and **white solid appears higher up** on the cooler part of the tube.
Safety: ammonia and hydrogen chloride are **irritant/toxic** gases, so do the experiment in a **fume cupboard** or with a small amount and good ventilation, wear eye protection.
Use this example to show that **the direction depends on the temperature**.
core.p: Ammonium chloride is a white solid. When it is heated in a test tube it breaks down (**thermal decomposition**) into two colourless gases, **ammonia** and **hydrogen chloride**. As the gases move up into the cooler part of the tube they react with each other and re-form **ammonium chloride**, which settles as a white solid on the cool glass. The forward reaction is **endothermic** and the reverse is **exothermic**. Because the white solid seems to move up the tube it can look like sublimation, but it is really a decomposition followed by a recombination, which shows the reaction is reversible.

bullets: **Haber process**: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); forward reaction **exothermic**.
**Dinitrogen tetroxide and nitrogen dioxide**: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g); colourless ⇌ brown, forward **endothermic**.
**Hydrated and anhydrous salts** (such as copper(II) sulfate and cobalt(II) chloride).
**Ammonium chloride** heating and cooling.
In unfamiliar examples you will be given the **energy change** or told which direction is exothermic, then asked to deduce the opposite direction.
Do not say that these reactions 'go backwards by themselves': the direction changes because of the **conditions**.
core.p: The Haber process is the most important example of a reversible reaction in the AQA specification: nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia, but ammonia also decomposes back into nitrogen and hydrogen. Other examples are sometimes used in exam questions as unfamiliar contexts, and you are expected to apply the same ideas: identify the ⇌ symbol, decide which direction is endothermic or exothermic, and explain how conditions affect the direction. The principle is always the same, so you do not need to memorise lots of different examples.

bullets: One-way reactions use up the **limiting reactant** completely; reversible reactions in closed systems do not.
In a reversible reaction the **percentage yield** is limited by the position of equilibrium.
Industry must choose **conditions** to maximise yield without making the process too slow or too expensive.
For reversible reactions in open containers (such as heating copper sulfate in an open tube), the **product can escape**, so the reverse reaction cannot occur.
If a question says a reaction is 'reversible', assume the **same energy** transfer in both directions.
Unreacted reactants in a reversible industrial process are usually **recycled** back into the reactor.
core.p: It helps to contrast reversible reactions with the many reactions that appear to go to completion. In a **one-way (irreversible) reaction**, the products are so stable that they do not change back to reactants under normal conditions, so the reactants are used up completely (if one reactant is limiting). Examples include burning fuels, rusting and neutralisation of a strong acid with an alkali. In a reversible reaction in a **closed system**, the reaction does not go to completion, so the mixture always contains both reactants and products, and this affects the **yield** of useful products in industry.

bullets: A **closed system** means no substances can enter or leave the reaction vessel.
At equilibrium both reactions continue, so the concentrations of reactants and products **stay constant**.
**Forward rate = reverse rate** at equilibrium (the rates are equal, not the concentrations).
The position of equilibrium depends on **temperature, pressure and concentration** (Higher tier).
A **catalyst** speeds up both directions equally, so it does not change the position of equilibrium but helps the system reach it faster.
In an **open system** (such as an open test tube) equilibrium is not reached because gases escape.
core.h: Closed systems and the link to dynamic equilibrium
core.p: When a reversible reaction takes place in a **closed system**, where no reactants or products can enter or leave, the forward and reverse reactions both continue and the mixture reaches **equilibrium**. At equilibrium the **rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction**. This is called a **dynamic equilibrium** because the reactions are still happening, but the amounts of reactants and products stay constant. The idea is covered in the next point of the specification, but you need to see that it follows directly from reversibility.

bullets: **Method**: heat blue crystals gently → they turn **white** and **steam/condensation** forms; **cool**; add **a few drops of water** → solid turns **blue** and the tube gets **warm**.
A **thermometer** or temperature probe can show the **temperature rise** when water is added (exothermic).

**Safety**: wear **eye protection**; copper(II) sulfate is **harmful** and an **irritant**; do not heat strongly; hold the tube with a **holder** and keep the mouth pointed away from people; allow equipment to **cool** before touching.
Use a **small amount** of solid to avoid spitting and to reduce hazards.
**Observation language**: 'the blue solid turned to a white powder' and 'the white powder turned blue and became warm'.
The test can be **repeated** several times to show that the reaction is truly reversible.
A mass measurement before and after heating shows **loss of mass** equal to the water driven off.
core.h: Investigating a reversible reaction in the lab
core.p: A simple demonstration of reversibility uses hydrated copper(II) sulfate. A small amount of the blue crystals is heated gently in a boiling tube, held at an angle with the mouth pointing away from people, until the solid turns white and condensation appears on the cooler part of the tube. After cooling, a few drops of water are added to the white solid and the colour change and temperature change are recorded. This shows both the forward reaction (endothermic) and the reverse reaction (exothermic) in one experiment.

bullets: **Rate** and **yield** often pull in opposite directions in reversible reactions.
**Compromise conditions** are chosen to give an acceptable rate and a reasonable yield at an acceptable cost.
**Unreacted** reactants are separated from the product and **recycled** to save raw materials.
The Haber process uses **about 450 °C, 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst** (conditions you meet in the 'Using resources' topic).
**Cooling** the gases lets the ammonia **liquefy** so it can be removed from the unreacted gases.
Understanding exothermic and endothermic directions is essential for **predicting** the effect of temperature on yield (Higher tier).
core.h: Why reversible reactions matter in industry
core.p: Many important industrial reactions are reversible, so the yield is limited. In the Haber process, for example, the reaction mixture leaving the reactor contains only some of the ammonia that could be made, and the remaining nitrogen and hydrogen are **recycled**. Engineers must choose conditions (temperature, pressure, catalyst) that give a good balance between the **rate** and the **equilibrium yield**. Because the forward Haber reaction is exothermic, a higher temperature speeds up the reaction but moves the equilibrium towards the reactants, giving a lower yield, which is why a compromise temperature is used.

bullets: **1 mark**: 'What does ⇌ mean?' → the reaction is **reversible** (products can react to re-form the reactants).
**1 or 2 marks**: 'State the energy change for the reverse reaction' → the **same amount**, but **endothermic** if the forward is exothermic (include the value and the sign).
**2 marks**: 'Describe what you would see' → give **colour change** and **temperature change** with direction.
**Link to energy changes (4.5)**: ΔH, activation energy, reaction profiles, bond energies.
**Link to rates (4.6.1)**: catalysts speed up both directions equally.
**Link to equilibrium and Le Chatelier (4.6.2.3 and 4.6.2.4, Higher tier)** and the **Haber process (4.10)**.
Always write **exothermic/endothermic** spelled correctly and never swap them: **exo = exits** (energy goes out).
core.h: Exam technique and links to other topics
core.p: Questions on this topic are usually short but they reward precise wording. You will be asked to give the meaning of ⇌, to state the energy change in the reverse direction, to describe observations in the copper sulfate or ammonium chloride experiment, or to link the topic to equilibrium and the Haber process. Use correct terminology (reversible, forward and reverse reaction, exothermic, endothermic, closed system) and always state that the same amount of energy is involved in both directions.

exam: **1 mark** 'What does the symbol ⇌ mean?': 'the reaction is reversible' / 'products can react to form the original reactants'.
**1 mark** 'Name the type of energy change in the reverse reaction': give **endothermic** if the forward is exothermic (and vice versa).
**2 marks** 'The forward reaction releases 50 kJ. State the energy change for the reverse': **50 kJ absorbed (endothermic)**; include both size and direction.
For **observations**, give the **colour change** with starting and finishing colours (blue → white, white → blue) and mention **temperature** (gets warm) or **steam**.
State the **chemical test for water**: 'anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue'.
For **ammonium chloride** answers: 'decomposes on heating to ammonia and hydrogen chloride; these react on cooling to re-form ammonium chloride (white solid) higher up the tube'.
Command words: **State** = brief fact; **Describe** = what you see happens; **Explain** = reasons ('because', 'so'); **Suggest** = apply to an unfamiliar situation.

**Reaction profile** questions: draw the same peak for both directions, label the energy change with an arrow, and state that the reverse activation energy is larger when the forward reaction is exothermic.
Mention **closed system** whenever the question asks about equilibrium.
Never write **'reversible reactions are reactions that can be undone by magic'**; use the board wording: 'the products can react to form the original reactants'.
Spell **exothermic** and **endothermic** correctly and write the sign of ΔH where needed.

mistakes.r: The direction depends on the conditions; the products can react to re-form the reactants when conditions change.
mistakes.w: A reversible reaction goes backwards on its own.

mistakes.r: The reverse is endothermic and the SAME amount of energy is transferred.
mistakes.w: If the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction releases less energy.
Using a single arrow → for a reversible reaction.

mistakes.r: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is white; the hydrated form is blue.
Heating hydrated copper sulfate (driving off water) is endothermic; adding water to anhydrous is exothermic.
mistakes.w: Heating hydrated copper sulfate is exothermic.

mistakes.r: It undergoes thermal decomposition into NH₃ and HCl, which recombine on cooling.
Equilibrium needs a closed system; in an open system the gases can escape.
mistakes.w: A reversible reaction always reaches equilibrium.

mistakes.r: Exothermic means energy is released to the surroundings and the temperature of the surroundings rises.
mistakes.w: Exothermic means the temperature of the reaction mixture is lower.

mistakes.r: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally.
mistakes.w: Catalysts make a reversible reaction go only forwards.

summary: You must know that in a reversible reaction the products can react to form the original reactants (shown by ⇌), that the direction can be changed by changing conditions, and that if the reaction is exothermic in one direction it is endothermic in the other with the same amount of energy transferred. Examples include hydrated copper(II) sulfate and ammonium chloride; the topic leads into dynamic equilibrium and the Haber process.

terms.d: A reaction in which the products can react to produce the original reactants.
The reaction in which the reactants on the left of ⇌ are converted into the products on the right.
The reaction in which the products are converted back into the original reactants.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Water molecules that are part of the structure of a crystal, in a fixed ratio.
A system in which no reactants or products can enter or leave.
A system in which substances can enter or leave, so gaseous products may escape.
The point in a reversible reaction in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
A reaction in which a substance is broken down into simpler substances by heating.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react.
The overall transfer of energy in a reaction: negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.
In a closed system, the point where the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant.

worked.ans: The reverse reaction is endothermic with ΔH = +92 kJ/mol.
worked.q: For the Haber process N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the forward reaction is exothermic with ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. State the type and size of energy change for the reverse reaction. (2 marks)
steps: In a reversible reaction, if one direction is exothermic the other is endothermic (1 mark).
The same amount of energy is transferred: 92 kJ/mol, but now absorbed (1 mark).

worked.ans: On heating, blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate turns white as water is driven off (endothermic). When water is added the white solid turns blue and the tube gets warm (exothermic). This shows a reversible reaction: CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O, with the same amount of energy transferred in each direction.
worked.q: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated in a test tube and then cooled. Water is added to the product. Describe the observations and explain what they show about the reaction. (4 marks)
steps: Heating: the blue solid turns to a white powder and steam/condensation is seen (1).
Adding water: the white powder turns blue again (1).
The tube becomes warm when water is added, so the reverse reaction is exothermic (1).
The forward reaction (heating) is endothermic; the reaction is reversible, with the same energy transferred in each direction (1).

worked.ans: Reverse activation energy = 100 kJ/mol; reverse ΔH = +40 kJ/mol (endothermic).
worked.q: A reversible reaction has a forward activation energy of 60 kJ/mol and a forward ΔH of −40 kJ/mol. Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction and its ΔH. (3 marks)
steps: Reverse ΔH has the same size but opposite sign: +40 kJ/mol (1).
The reverse reaction starts 40 kJ/mol lower than the reactants, so it must climb to the same peak: Ea(reverse) = 60 + 40 (1).
